acqinfo.head: Acquisition Information
acqinfo.p: These items came to the Library of Virginia in shipments of court papers from Chesterfield County in an undated accession. One record came to the Library of Virginia in accession number 33513.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Prior to 2026, the judgement descriptive records were not standardized in their inclusion of contextual information or content lists. Local Records staff reviewed this record and have updated to current standards as of 2026.

The Chesterfield County Judgment of the College of William and Mary vs. John W. Tomlin, 1813 was previously described separately. This judgment is included in this record, but are still described separately in the Library catalog.
Encoded by G. Crawford: 2010; updated by J. Taylor: August 2026.

bioghist.head: Historical Information
bioghist.p: Context for Record Type: Judgments are identified as civil suits, often involving debt, heard by a jury on the "law" side of the court as opposed to the "chancery" (or equity) side. Should the defendant not have funds to repay the debt, the court ordered their property (including enslaved people) to be seized and sold to repay the debt owed to the plaintiff. Judgments also contain suits brought by enslaved people seeking to gain their freedom.

In Judgments, an assumpsit or declaration (sometimes referred to as a narratio) lays out the plaintiff's grievance as a petition acted as a formal application to the court requesting judicial action. Judgment suits also generally included record types like subpoenas, summons, and exhibit. Judgments may also include additional documentations such as executions, bonds, and various kinds of writs.

Judgment suits make up a large quantity of a locality's records; consequently, they provide a great deal of information concerning the activities and interests of the people who lived in the locality. Since the vast majority of judgment suits relate to financial matters, they are a valuable resource in studying the economic and social history of Virginia localities and are the impotence for many chancery suits.

Locality History: Chesterfield County was named for Philip Dormer Stanhope, fourth earl of Chesterfield, British statesman and diplomat, and was formed from Henrico County in 1749. The county seat is Chesterfield Court House. Part of Henrico County was added to Chesterfield in 1922.

Ejectments are a formal court order that declares the property owner to be the rightful owner of a piece of land or building and legally removes the unauthorized occupant. The court might also declare financial damages for the lost use of the property.
Office judgments are ruled on outside of a traditional court hearing by a court clerk, rather than a judge and usually occurs when a defendant failed to file a timely response.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content
scopecontent.p: Chesterfield County (Va.) Judgments, 1749-1955 contains civil cases in which justice was administered on the strictly formulated rules of common law. The majority of cases in this record series relate to matters of debt. These records consist of both processed and unprocessed loose records and several volumes.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p:
This collection is arranged into three series:
Series I: Judgments, 1749-1914
Series II: Unprocessed Judgments, 1769-1927
Series III: Judgment Volumes, 1809-1955

relatedmaterial.head: Related Material
relatedmaterial.p: Additional Chesterfield County Court Records can be found on microfilm at The Library of Virginia web site. Consult "A Guide to Virginia County and City Records on Microfilm."

scopecontent.p: This series is organized chronologically by year.

Included in these records is the suit of the College of William and Mary vs. John W. Tomlin from 1813. This suit was an ejectment suit involving property owned by the plaintiff in King William County and Tomlin was a tenant. College of William and Mary accused Tomlin of violating the rental agreement between the two by cutting trees for personal gain and failure to pay rent on schedule. The suit includes three indentures used as exhibits.

All records in this record series are unprocessed and remain tri-folded within their original bundles; the bundles also include other court records, such as commonwealth causes, road and bridge records, tax and fiscal records, Overseers of the Poor, etc. Not all record types will be found in every bundle of papers. The contents of the boxes are not arranged in any particular order and dates may overlap between boxes. Some records may be fragile.
